title: `add_url_rule` leaves a route registered even after an endpoint conflict
body:
## Description
‘add_url_rule’ correctly raises an error when an endpoint already exists and you try to register a different view function with the same endpoint.

However, after you catch the error and continue running the code, the URL you tried to add (/b, for example) still exists. When a user requests /b, it is routed to the view function that was already registered for that endpoint, rather than the new view function whose registration failed.

## Example

```python
from flask import Flask

app = Flask(__name__)

def first():
    return "first"

def second():
    return "second"

app.add_url_rule("/a", endpoint="same", view_func=first)

try:
    app.add_url_rule("/b", endpoint="same", view_func=second)
except AssertionError as e:
    print(e)

client = app.test_client()

print(client.get("/a").status_code, client.get("/a").data)
print(client.get("/b").status_code, client.get("/b").data)
```

### Expected Result

```text
View function mapping is overwriting an existing endpoint fun

title: `stream_with_context`: abandoned generator leaves the app context current on the worker thread; later requests skip `teardown_appcontext`
body:
`stream_with_context` pushes the request's contexts onto whichever thread iterates the response body, and pops them only if the generator completes or is closed on that same thread. When a client disconnects mid-stream, the server abandons the body iterator and GC finalizes it later — often on a different thread. That cross-context pop fails (`LookupError`/`ValueError` from `ContextVar.reset`, swallowed as "Exception ignored in ..."), and the app context stays current on the worker thread.

Because `RequestContext.push` reuses an ambient app context of the same app, every later request on that pooled thread runs under the stuck context and `teardown_appcontext` never fires for it. Anything keyed to the app context then leaks once per thread for the life of the process — with Flask-SQLAlchemy that is one connection held idle-in-transaction per poisoned thread, with nothing in the logs.

Related: #5774 fixed the same cross-context token failure for async views; #5804 covers teardown orde

title: jsonify emits NaN and Infinity, which are not valid JSON
body:
`jsonify` serialises `float("nan")` and `float("inf")` as the bare literals `NaN` and `Infinity`. Those are not valid JSON (RFC 8259 allows only decimal numbers), so the response is served as `application/json` but cannot be parsed by a strict parser, including the browser's `JSON.parse`.

This inherits from `json.dumps`, whose `allow_nan` defaults to `True`. `DefaultJSONProvider` sets `default`, `ensure_ascii` and `sort_keys`, but never touches `allow_nan`, so the permissive default applies.

The path to it is ordinary: any average, ratio or division that can meet an empty input produces `nan` without anything looking wrong on the server.

Replication:

```python
from flask import Flask, jsonify

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route("/stats")
def stats():
    values = []
    mean = sum(values) / len(values) if values else float("nan")
    return jsonify({"count": len(values), "mean": mean})

with app.test_client() as c:
    r = c.get("/stats")
    print(r.headers["Content-Type"])      #

title: Confusing docstring in Flask.get_send_file_max_age and Flask.send_static_file
body:

- `Flask.send_static_file`

title: Tests fail with pytest 9.1: _pytest.monkeypatch.notset removed
body:
Flask's test suite imports the private notset sentinel from _pytest.monkeypatch in both tests/conftest.py and tests/test_cli.py. pytest 9.1 removed this attribute, moving it to _pytest.compat.NOTSET. This causes a collection-time crash — no tests can run at all.

### Reproducing
```
pip install -e . pytest==9.1.1
pytest tests/
tests/test_cli.py:14: in <module>
    from _pytest.monkeypatch import notset
E   ImportError: cannot import name 'notset' from '_pytest.monkeypatch'
```
Even after fixing test_cli.py, every test fails because tests/conftest.py accesses monkeypatch.notset as a module attribute in the _standard_os_environ session fixture:

`tests/conftest.py:19: AttributeError: module '_pytest.monkeypatch' has no attribute 'notset'`
### Expected Behavior
The test suite should work with pytest 9.1+.

### Environment:

Python version: 3.15.0b2
Flask version: 3.1.3

title: Add a query() route shortcut and MethodView support for HTTP QUERY (RFC 10008)
body:
The HTTP `QUERY` method was standardized in
[RFC 10008](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc10008/) (June 2026): a safe,
idempotent request method that carries content in the request body (the
standardized replacement for the "use POST for a read-only query with a large
body" workaround in GraphQL / REST search APIs).

I'd like Flask to treat `QUERY` as a first-class method like the others:

- a `query()` route shortcut on `Scaffold` (inherited by `Flask` and
  `Blueprint`), mirroring `get`/`post`/`put`/`delete`/`patch`;
- `MethodView` dispatch of `QUERY` to a `query` handler (add `"query"` to
  `views.http_method_funcs`).

---

Is this solvable without changes to Flask? Partly — `@app.route("/x",
methods=["QUERY"])` already works today, since Flask doesn't restrict method
names and Werkzeug parses the body. What's missing is the ergonomic shortcut and
`MethodView` dispatch that every other common method already has, so this is a
consistency/ergonomics gap rather than new capability — t

title: register_blueprint name override bypasses dot validation
body:
The `Blueprint` constructor explicitly prevents dots in names (`if "." in name: raise ValueError`) because dots denote nested blueprints. However, `app.register_blueprint(..., name="...")` doesn't enforce this check on the overridden name.

If a blueprint is registered with a dot via the `name` kwarg, it bypasses the restriction. This tricks the framework into treating it as a nested blueprint, causing the parent's callbacks (like `before_request`) to unexpectedly execute for the unrelated child blueprint.

### How to replicate the bug
```python
import flask

app = flask.Flask(__name__)
parent = flask.Blueprint("parent", __name__)
child = flask.Blueprint("child", __name__)

parent.before_request(lambda: setattr(flask.g, "hit", True))
child.add_url_rule("/", "index", lambda: str(hasattr(flask.g, "hit")))

app.register_blueprint(parent)
app.register_blueprint(child, name="parent.fake") # Bypasses dot validation

print(app.test_client().get("/").get_data(as_text=True))

title: Config.from_file() silently ignores fewer OSError codes than from_pyfile()
body:
## Summary

`Config.from_file()` and `Config.from_pyfile()` behave inconsistently when `silent=True` and an `OSError` is raised.

`from_pyfile()` silences errors for these `errno` codes:

```python
if silent and e.errno in (errno.ENOENT, errno.EISDIR, errno.ENOTDIR):
    return False
```

But `from_file()` only silences:

```python
if silent and e.errno in (errno.ENOENT, errno.EISDIR):
    return False
```

It is missing `errno.ENOTDIR`.

## Reproduction

`ENOTDIR` is raised when a path component is a regular file, not a directory. For example, if `/tmp/myconfig` is a regular file and you try to open `/tmp/myconfig/settings.json`, the OS raises `ENOTDIR` (not a directory).

title: FLASK_DEBUG env variable no longer works as of click 8.4.0
body:
**Description of bug:**

FLASK_DEBUG=1 was working previously to set flask's debug mode either in a .env/.flaskenv and using python-dotenv OR by manually setting with export FLASK_DEBUG=1. As of today, setting it by env variable no longer works. Flask will still use debug mode using the --debug flag. Downgrading click to 8.3.3 resolves the issue.

**Replicate bug:**

```
python3 -m venv venv
. venv/bin/activate
pip install flask
cat << EOF > app.py
from flask import Flask
app = Flask(__name__)
@app.route('/')
def index():
    return 'hello world'
EOF
export FLASK_DEBUG=1
flask run
```

**This produces:**

Debug mode: off

```
pip install click==8.3.3
flask run
```

**Then produces:**

Debug mode: on

**Environment:**

- Python version: 3.12.3
- Flask version: 3.1.3

title: Config.from_file() silently ignores fewer OSError codes than from_pyfile()
body:
## Summary

`Config.from_file()` and `Config.from_pyfile()` behave inconsistently when `silent=True` and an `OSError` is raised.

`from_pyfile()` silences errors for these `errno` codes:

```python
if silent and e.errno in (errno.ENOENT, errno.EISDIR, errno.ENOTDIR):
    return False
```

But `from_file()` only silences:

```python
if silent and e.errno in (errno.ENOENT, errno.EISDIR):
    return False
```

It is missing `errno.ENOTDIR`.

## Reproduction

`ENOTDIR` is raised when a path component is a regular file, not a directory. For example, if `/tmp/myconfig` is a regular file and you try to open `/tmp/myconfig/settings.json`, the OS raises `ENOTDIR` (not a directory).

```python
import os, tempfile
from flask import Flask

app = Flask(__name__)

# create a file where we expect a directory
with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(delete=False, suffix="cfg") as f:
    f.write(b"")
    tmp = f.name

# from_pyfile with silent=True returns False (correct)
result = app.config.from_pyfile(tmp +

title: Add a query() route shortcut and MethodView support for HTTP QUERY (RFC 10008)
body:
The HTTP `QUERY` method was standardized in
[RFC 10008](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc10008/) (June 2026): a safe,
idempotent request method that carries content in the request body (the
standardized replacement for the "use POST for a read-only query with a large
body" workaround in GraphQL / REST search APIs).

I'd like Flask to treat `QUERY` as a first-class method like the others:

- a `query()` route shortcut on `Scaffold` (inherited by `Flask` and
  `Blueprint`), mirroring `get`/`post`/`put`/`delete`/`patch`;
- `MethodView` dispatch of `QUERY` to a `query` handler (add `"query"` to
  `views.http_method_funcs`).

---

Is this solvable without changes to Flask? Partly — `@app.route("/x",
methods=["QUERY"])` already works today, since Flask doesn't restrict method
names and Werkzeug parses the body. What's missing is the ergonomic shortcut and
`MethodView` dispatch that every other common method already has, so this is a
consistency/ergonomics gap rather than new capability — t
